source_work: Shodo Harada Roshi, inscription on an ensō poster given to Jon Kabat-Zinn at Tahoma Zen Monastery, Whidbey Island, 11 September 2001; recounted by Kabat-Zinn on the Mind & Life podcast "The Heart of Mindfulness"
notes: Harada Roshi handed out the ensō poster on 11 September 2001; Kabat-Zinn retells it in the Inquiring Mind interview. Verified: In the Mind & Life podcast transcript Kabat-Zinn describes the Zen-circle calligraphy Harada Roshi gave him that day and quotes the inscription: "Never forget the 1000 year view."

quote: Psychotherapie versucht die Dinge im Raum neu anzuordnen, Meditation hilft den Raum zu verlassen.
author: Ram Dass
source_work: Psychotherapy and Meditation: A Forum, Inquiring Mind 5:1, Sommer 1988
notes: German rendering of Ram Dass's answer in the Inquiring Mind forum; English original filed alongside. Renders the source loosely: A free German shortening of the attested wording "Western psychotherapy rearranges the furniture in the room, Eastern techniques help you get out of the room" (inquiringmind.com).

quote: Menschen tun nur zwei Dinge - entweder sie senden Liebe oder sie fragen danach.
source_work: A Course in Miracles, Text, Kapitel 12.I.3
notes: Paraphrase of the Course in Miracles teaching that every act is either an extension of love or a call for love; no named author. Renders the source loosely: A faithful summary of "Every loving thought is true. Everything else is an appeal for healing and help, regardless of the form it takes." (Wikisource, the text of A Course in Miracles).

quote: Everyone you meet always asks if you have a career, are married, or own a house as if life was some kind of grocery list. But no one ever asks you if you are happy.
author: Heath Ledger
notes: Attribution unverified: Nothing resembling this appears in Ledger's filmed or printed interviews before his death in 2008, and no contemporaneous source carries it; it began circulating as a social-media caption roughly a decade later, which is where the attribution appears to originate.

quote: Stop trying to control everything and just let go. Let go!
author: Tyler Durden
source_work: Fight Club (dir. David Fincher, 1999), screenplay by Jim Uhls, the car-crash scene
notes: Spoken by the character Tyler Durden. Previously attributed to Chuck Palahniuk. Reattributed: The line is Tyler's in the film, not in Palahniuk's novel: the corresponding chapter has a Project Mayhem mechanic swerving into oncoming traffic with no "let go" instruction, so the line belongs to the film and not to the book. Screenplay by Jim Uhls.

quote: You're not your job. You're not how much money you have in the bank. You're not the car you drive. You're not the contents of your wallet. You're not your fucking khakis. You're the all-singing, all-dancing crap of the world.
author: Chuck Palahniuk
source_work: Chuck Palahniuk, Fight Club (W. W. Norton, 1996), ch. 17 (Tyler's address to fight club)
notes: Spoken by the character Tyler Durden. Renders the source loosely: The novel reads "You are not your job... You are all singing, all dancing crap of the world"; the bank keeps the smoother 1999 film phrasing, which says the same thing.

quote: People's lives become what they think is possible.
author: Roger Mills
notes: Attribution unverified: The line is credited to Mills by the Center for Sustainable Change, which he co-founded, but no page or passage in his published Health Realization writing could be located to support it.

quote: If it's out of your hands, it deserves freedom from your mind too.
author: Ivan Nuru
notes: Attribution unverified: Nuru is a social-media writer with no published collection carrying this line; every occurrence traces back to reposts and aggregators.

quote: The way you speak to yourself matters.
notes: Attributed to Unknown in source. Attribution unverified: A generic self-talk maxim with no traceable origin; the nearest sourced relative is Brené Brown's "Talk to yourself like you would to someone you love" in The Gifts of Imperfection (2010).

quote: Visualise your highest self and start showing up as him.
author: Ali Owens
notes: Attribution unverified: The wording appears in a blog post by Ali Owens as one item in a list of quotations she had collected, so the page does not establish her authorship, and no earlier source could be found.

quote: To fall in love with yourself is the first secret to happiness.
author: Robert Morley
notes: Source spells 'Morely'. Attribution unverified: Quotation sites credit Morley's memoir Responsible Gentleman (1966), but no text of that book could be checked and the longer circulating version ("then if you're not a good mixer you can always fall back on your own company") is equally uncited.

quote: The first and best victory is to conquer self.
author: Plato
notes: Verified: Greek from the Perseus text of the Laws; the words are spoken by Cleinias in the dialogue’s opening exchange.

quote: Educating the mind without educating the heart is no education at all.
author: Aristotle
notes: Attribution unverified: A well-documented pseudo-Aristotle line found nowhere in the corpus and carrying no source on Wikiquote’s Aristotle page.

quote: A mind is like a parachute. It doesn't work if it isn't open.
author: Thomas Robert Dewar (Lord Dewar)
source_work: Saying attributed to Lord Dewar from the 1920s; earliest known printed instances date to 1927
notes: Previously attributed to Frank Zappa. Reattributed: The line is absent from The Real Frank Zappa Book and from Zappa's documented interviews, and Quote Investigator's history of "the mind is like a parachute" shows it circulating as Lord Dewar's more than a decade before Zappa was born.

quote: When you focus on the good, the good gets better.
author: Abraham Hicks
notes: Attribution unverified: A fair summary of the Abraham-Hicks teaching, but no dated workshop recording or book page carrying this exact sentence could be located in the Hicks material searched.

quote: In a world full of doing, doing, doing, it's important to take a moment to just breathe, to just be.
notes: Attributed to Unknown in source. Attribution unverified: Searched the Internet Archive full-text corpus for 'to just breathe, to just be' and for 'a world full of doing': the only printed hit is an unrelated sentence in Trisha Cull's The Death of Small Creatures (2015). Everywhere else the line appears on wellness blogs and quote aggregators only, always unattributed.

quote: Your calm mind is the ultimate weapon against your challenges. So relax.
author: Bryant McGill
source_work: Bryant McGill, Simple Reminders aphorism; quoted verbatim and credited to him in Lynn A. Robinson, Put Your Intuition to Work (Conari Press, 2016), and in Alexandra Bernard-Simmons, Think Like a Boss (2016)
notes: Verified: The wording is identical in both printed books and the attribution is consistent. McGill's own titles (Voice of Reason, Simple Reminders) are not full-text searchable in the Internet Archive, so the first publication could not be pinned to a page.

quote: The still waters of a lake reflect the beauty around it. When the mind is still, the beauty of the self is reflected.
author: B.K.S. Iyengar
source_work: Quoted and credited to B.K.S. Iyengar in Swami Sivananda Radha, Hatha Yoga: The Hidden Language (Timeless Books, 1995), in the chapter on Hamsa
notes: Previously attributed to Vanda Scaravelli. Reattributed: In the Internet Archive corpus the sentence occurs only as an Iyengar quotation, the earliest in Radha's 1995 book, a decade before Iyengar's Light on Life. Nothing of the kind turns up under Vanda Scaravelli's name; her attribution appears only on quote aggregators.

quote: Just when you feel you have no time to relax, know this is the moment you most need to relax.
author: Matt Haig
source_work: Reasons to Stay Alive (Canongate, 2015), item 39 of the closing list 'How to live'
notes: Renders the source loosely: Haig's sentence reads: 'Just when you feel you have no time to relax, know that this is the moment you most need to make time to relax.' The bank's line drops 'make time to' but misstates nothing, so it is kept as collected.

quote: Worrying is stupid, it's like walking around with an umbrella waiting for it to rain.
notes: Attributed to Unknown in source. Attribution unverified: No printed occurrence anywhere in the Internet Archive corpus. Online it is universally credited to Wiz Khalifa and was quoted as his in an October 2015 tweet by the football coach Randy Edsall, but no original tweet, lyric or interview could be traced, so the bank's 'Unknown' stands.

quote: No matter how difficult the past, you can always begin again today.
author: Jack Kornfield
source_work: Jack Kornfield, Buddha's Little Instruction Book (Bantam, 1994)
notes: Verified: Anni Daulter's Sacred Relationship (2017) credits Kornfield by name and Anne I. Eason's IEP and Inclusion Tips (2006) cites Buddha's Little Instruction Book. Because of that title the line is very often re-attributed to the Buddha himself, as in T. Alexander Anderson's The Gift of Time (2001).

quote: Feelings come and go like clouds in a windy sky. Conscious breathing is my anchor.
author: Thích Nhất Hạnh
source_work: Present Moment, Wonderful Moment, gatha "Adjusting Posture"
notes: Renders gatha 17 of the Vietnamese originals Từng Bước Nở Hoa Sen and Bước Tới Thảnh Thơi.

quote: Believe you can, and you're halfway there.
author: Theodore Roosevelt
notes: Attribution unverified: Nothing of the kind occurs in Roosevelt's speeches, letters or books. Every one of the ninety occurrences in the Internet Archive corpus is a recent quotation anthology, planner or gift book carrying his name with no source; Quote Investigator has no article on it. It reads as a twentieth-century motivational coinage that acquired his name.

quote: The mind is like water. When it's turbulent, it's difficult to see. When it's calm, everything becomes clear.
author: Prasad Mahes
notes: Attribution unverified: Neither the sentence nor the name 'Prasad Mahes' occurs anywhere in the Internet Archive corpus. The water-and-mind simile is a stock Zen-flavoured aphorism carried only by quote aggregators, and no person of that name could be traced as its author.

quote: Sometimes the bad things that happen in our lives put us directly on the path to the most wonderful things that will ever happen to us.
author: Nicole Reed
source_work: Nicole Reed, Ruining You (2013), spoken to Jay in dialogue late in the novel
notes: Wording as collected was: Sometimes the bad things that happen in our lives put us directly on the path to the best things that will ever happen to us. Wording corrected against the source: The novel's text reads 'the most wonderful things', not 'the best things': confirmed against the full online text of Ruining You, where a male character says it to Jay after she asks about going through hell to get a piece of heaven. The altered version has spread far enough to be reprinted in several later books.

quote: We cannot become what we need to be by remaining what we are.
author: Max De Pree
source_work: Max De Pree, Leadership Is an Art (Michigan State University Press, 1987)
notes: Source spells 'Max Depree'. Wording as collected was: We cannot become what we want by remaining what we are. Wording corrected against the source: 'We cannot become what we need to be by remaining what we are' returns over two hundred printed occurrences in the Internet Archive corpus, several crediting De Pree directly; 'what we want' returns none. The substitution weakens the point from necessity to preference.

quote: You are the sky. Everything else is just the weather.
author: Pema Chödrön
notes: Also collected as: You are the sky. Everything else - it's just the weather. Pema Chodron's line twice, with the author's name spelled two ways. The correctly spelled record is kept. Attribution unverified: Not in When Things Fall Apart, whose full text was checked, and not in any Chodron title in the Internet Archive corpus. The sentence surfaces only in quote anthologies from 2015 and 2016 (365 Thoughts on the Path of Buddha; Cher Kaufmann's Joy), usually as 'You are the sky. Everything else - it's just the weather.' The sky-and-weather image is genuinely hers, this formulation could not be sourced.

quote: Everything is created twice - first in your mind and then in the outside world.
author: Robin Sharma
source_work: Robin S. Sharma, MegaLiving! 30 Days to a Perfect Life (1995; 2005 printing checked)
notes: Wording as collected was: Everything is created twice. First in the mind and then in reality. Wording corrected against the source: Sharma's own book reads 'in the outside world'; 'first in the mind and then in reality' comes from mindfulness gift books (The Pocket Book of Mindfulness, 2015; Art for Mindfulness, 2015) quoting him second-hand. The underlying idea is older, Stephen Covey's 'all things are created twice'.

quote: Almost everything will work again if you unplug it for a few minutes. Including you.
author: Anne Lamott
source_work: Anne Lamott, 'Twelve truths I learned from life and writing', Facebook post of April 2015, reprinted in Salon and delivered as a TED talk in 2017
notes: Verified: Lamott punctuates it as a single sentence, 'Almost everything will work again if you unplug it for a few minutes, including you'; the bank's full stop before 'Including you' is a stylistic variant that circulates widely and changes nothing. Printed reprints (Suze Yalof Schwartz, Unplug, 2017) carry the comma form.

quote: Nature does not hurry, yet everything is accomplished.
author: Lao Tzu
notes: Attribution unverified: Not in any of the 81 chapters; a modern aphorism that merely echoes 無為而無不為, flagged as false in Wikiquote's Laozi misattributed section.

quote: Be happy in the moment, that's enough. Each moment is all we need, not more.
author: Mother Teresa
notes: Source spells 'Mother Theresa'. Attribution unverified: The earliest printed occurrence in the Internet Archive corpus is Patrick Lindsay's quotation compilation High Hopes (2014), which credits Mother Teresa but gives no source; the rest are colouring and gift books from 2015 on. Nothing resembling it appears in her own published writings in the corpus, and Quote Investigator has no entry.

quote: The present moment is filled with joy and happiness. If you are attentive, you will see it.
author: Thích Nhất Hạnh
source_work: Thich Nhat Hanh, Peace Is Every Step: The Path of Mindfulness in Everyday Life (Bantam, 1991), p. 22
notes: Written in English for Bantam; the Vietnamese edition is expressly a translation from the English, so this is the original wording. Verified: The wording is confirmed verbatim by books quoting the passage, including Stanislaus Kennedy's Day by Day (2013 and 2016) and Sreechinth C's Thich Nhat Hanh Quotes (2017), one of which shows it following the 'cookie of our childhood' passage that is unmistakably from this book. Peace Is Every Step itself is not full-text searchable, so the page rests on the bank's own citation.

quote: Every grain of experience is food for the greedy growing soul of the artist.
author: Anthony Burgess
source_work: Anthony Burgess, Here Comes Everybody: An Introduction to James Joyce for the Ordinary Reader (Faber, 1965), the chapter 'Martyr and Maze-maker'; published in the United States as Re Joyce
notes: Verified: Both printings carry the sentence verbatim in the discussion of A Portrait of the Artist as a Young Man; Harold Bloom's 1988 casebook on the Portrait and Jack Hendriksen's 1993 study both quote it from Burgess.

quote: We will be reminded - once more - that love is a skill, not an emotion.
author: The School of Life
notes: Attribution unverified: No occurrence in the Internet Archive corpus and none in The School of Life: An Emotional Education. theschooloflife.com returns 403 to automated requests and paywalls its article bodies, so the sentence could not be tied to a particular essay. The School of Life's standard formulation is 'love is a skill, not a feeling', which suggests this is a newsletter or social-media rewording.

quote: The emotionally intelligent person knows that love is a skill, not a feeling, and will require trust, vulnerability, generosity, humour, and selective resignation.
author: The School of Life
source_work: Alain de Botton, The School of Life: An Emotional Education (School of Life Press, 2019), the opening section defining emotional intelligence; the same passage is on alaindebotton.com
notes: Renders the source loosely: The original list runs 'trust, vulnerability, generosity, humour, sexual understanding and selective resignation'. The bank's version drops 'sexual understanding' and is otherwise word for word, so it is kept as collected. The book is signed by de Botton but published as the School of Life's house text, so the bank's institutional attribution is defensible.

quote: We will still be anxious when we finally have the house, the relationship and the right income.
author: The School of Life
notes: Attribution unverified: No printed occurrence, and none of the School of Life's readable anxiety or pessimism articles ('On Pessimism', 'The True Cause of Dread and Anxiety', 'Four Ways of Coping With Anxiety') carries the sentence. The site refuses automated requests and paywalls most article bodies, so it could not be placed; the sentiment is characteristic but the wording is untraced.

quote: When you realise nothing is lacking, the whole world belongs to you.
author: Lao Tzu
notes: Renders the source loosely: Stephen Mitchell's free rendering of ch. 44 (Chinese from the Wikisource 匯校版 Laozi), not a translation of any line.

quote: One who conquers others is strong. One who conquers himself is all-powerful.
author: Lao Tzu
notes: Verified: Faithful rendering by Jonathan Star (Tarcher/Penguin, verse 33), matching the Wikisource Chinese text.

quote: One who approaches life with force surely gets something. One who remains content where he is surely gets everything.
author: Lao Tzu
notes: Renders the source loosely: Jonathan Star's verse 33 reorders these two clauses and adds "surely gets something/everything", which is absent from the Chinese.

quote: Complete the task at hand. Be selfless in your actions. This is the way of Heaven. This is the way to Heaven.
author: Lao Tzu
notes: Renders the source loosely: Jonathan Star's verse 9; his added pun "This is the way to Heaven" has no counterpart in the Wikisource Chinese.

quote: Life is a balance of holding on and letting go.
author: Rumi
notes: Attribution unverified: Absent from Barks' corpus and from the Persian Divan and Masnavi; a modern greeting-card aphorism with no Persian counterpart.

quote: Who you are is always right.
author: Deng Ming-Dao
source_work: Deng Ming-Dao, Everyday Tao: Living with Balance and Harmony (HarperSanFrancisco, 1996), in the passage on reading everything in relation to one's own personal Tao
notes: Attributed to Unknown in source. Previously attributed to no one. Reattributed: The sentence occurs exactly once in the entire Internet Archive corpus, inside Deng's own prose: 'its meaning in relation to your own personal Tao. Who you are is always right. Ultimately, your life and your relationship to Tao are solely a matter...'. A single occurrence in millions of books is the best available evidence of origin, though the bank may well have picked the line up already detached from it.

quote: Let go, or be dragged.
notes: Zen proverb; attributed to Unknown in source. Attribution unverified: Printed often but always as an anonymous proverb: Ronnie McBrayer's May the Road Rise to Meet You (2015) has it from a horseman as 'a most picturesque proverb', and Guy McPherson's Going Dark (2013) labels it 'a bit of Zen'. It is not in the Zen literature and no author could be found, so the bank's 'Unknown' is right.

quote: What the superior man seeks is in himself; what the small man seeks is in others.
author: Confucius
notes: Verified: Legge's exact translation of a genuine passage, verified against the Chinese Wikisource text of the Analects.

quote: If you are depressed, you are living in the past. If you are anxious, you are living in the future. If you are at peace, you are living in the present.
notes: Modern saying frequently misattributed to Lao Tzu; earliest forms anonymous (cf. Rev. Run, Words of Wisdom, 2006). Attribution unverified: The bank's 'Unknown' is the safe reading. The line is most often printed as Lao Tzu (Cher Kaufmann's Peace, 2017, among others) but it is nowhere in the Tao Te Ching, and every printed occurrence is a recent mindfulness or self-help book. No earlier or attributable source was found.

quote: Act without expectation.
author: Lao Tzu
notes: Attribution unverified: Listed among the fake Lao Tzu quotes by Stefan Stenudd (taoistic.com); it condenses the idea of 為而不恃 (ch. 10) but translates no actual line.

quote: Rest and be kind, you don't have to prove anything.
author: Jack Kerouac
source_work: Jack Kerouac, The Dharma Bums (Viking, 1958), Ray Smith's thought to himself in the mountains late in the novel
notes: Verified: The 1958 text and the 1973, 1990 and 2006 printings all read: '"Besides," I thought, "rest and be kind, you don't have to prove anything."' The bank has the words exactly, though in the book they are a passing thought rather than a maxim. Winifred Hindley quoted it as Kerouac's as early as 1968.

quote: Don't try to steer the river.
author: Deepak Chopra
source_work: Deepak Chopra, The Seven Spiritual Laws of Success for Parents (Harmony, 1997), in the passage beginning 'the ultimate organizer is Nature'
notes: Verified: All three Internet Archive printings (1997, 1999, 2006) read 'that the ultimate organizer is Nature. Don't try to steer the river. When Nature is most productive...', so the sentence is Chopra's own and the bank has it exactly.

quote: Be the change that you wish to see in the world.
author: Arleen Lorrance
notes: Source spells 'Ghandi'. Previously attributed to Mahatma Gandhi. Reattributed: Quote Investigator traces this wording to Arleen Lorrance; Gandhi's actual sentence was "If we could change ourselves, the tendencies in the world would also change" (Indian Opinion, 9 August 1913; CWMG vol. 13).

quote: In a gentle way, you can shake the world.
author: Mahatma Gandhi
notes: Source spells 'Ghandi'. Attribution unverified: Absent from the 100 volumes of the Collected Works of Mahatma Gandhi and from every sourced compilation; it appears only in uncited modern quote collections.

quote: The weak can never forgive. Forgiveness is the attribute of the strong.
author: Mahatma Gandhi
source_work: Young India, 2 April 1931, reporting Gandhi's statement to the press at Karachi, 23 March 1931
notes: Source spells 'Ghandi'. Verbatim in CWMG vol. 51, from Gandhi's Karachi press interview on the execution of Bhagat Singh, published in his English weekly, so this is the original wording. Verified: Printed Gandhi collections cite the line to Young India, matching the bank's citation: Jenny Youngman's Grad's Pocket Guide to Greatness gives 'Mohandas Gandhi, Young India', and The Book of Gandhi Wisdom (1995) carries it. The wording is stable across all occurrences.

quote: An eye for an eye only ends up making the whole world blind.
author: Mahatma Gandhi
notes: Source spells 'Ghandi'. Attribution unverified: Not found in Gandhi's writings; the Yale Book of Quotations and Gandhi scholar Dennis Dalton find no instance, and the epigram is attested independently by 1914.

quote: You must not lose faith in humanity. Humanity is an ocean; if a few drops of the ocean are dirty, the ocean does not become dirty.
author: Mahatma Gandhi
source_work: Letter to Rajkumari Amrit Kaur, 29 August 1947, in The Collected Works of Mahatma Gandhi
notes: Source spells 'Ghandi'. Gandhi's correspondence with Amrit Kaur was in English, so this is the original wording. Verified: The bank's citation holds up: the 1947 letter to Kaur, who was Gandhi's correspondent and later India's first health minister, is the source given wherever the line is traced rather than merely repeated. The wording, including 'Humanity is an ocean', is stable in printed occurrences going back to at least 1965.

quote: Forgiveness is choosing to love. It is the first skill of self-giving love.
author: Mahatma Gandhi
notes: Source credits Mohandas Gandhi. Attribution unverified: Not in CWMG or any sourced compilation; the devotional idiom is alien to Gandhi's English and it surfaces only on quote aggregators.

quote: If you have the ability to love, love yourself first.
author: Charles Bukowski
source_work: "how to be a great writer", in: Love Is a Dog from Hell (1977), pp. 92-93
notes: Verified: Found verbatim in the book text ("and if you have the ability to love / love yourself first"); bank gives an accurate prose excerpt.

quote: Find what you love and let it kill you.
author: Kinky Friedman
notes: Previously attributed to Charles Bukowski. Reattributed: Not in any Bukowski text I could search; Quote Investigator and the Bukowski Forum trace the line to Kinky Friedman, and Wikiquote does not list it among his quotes.

quote: What matters most is how well you walk through the fire.
author: Charles Bukowski
source_work: "how is your heart?", closing lines; verified in The Pleasures of the Damned: Poems 1951-1993 (2007)
notes: Verified: The poem ends "what matters most is / how well you / walk through the / fire"; the line later titled the 1999 Black Sparrow collection.

quote: Sometimes you climb out of bed in the morning and you think, I'm not going to make it, but you laugh inside - remembering all the times you've felt that way.
author: Charles Bukowski
source_work: "gamblers all", in: The Night Torn Mad with Footsteps: New Poems (2001)
notes: Verified: Opening lines match the book text word for word; bank only adds a dash.

quote: And yet women - good women - frightened me because they eventually wanted your soul, and what was left of mine, I wanted to keep.
author: Charles Bukowski
notes: Verified: Verbatim in the novel text; note it is Chinaski's first-person narration, not a detached aphorism.

quote: The free soul is rare, but you know it when you see it - basically because you feel good, very good, when you are near or with them.
author: Charles Bukowski
source_work: "A Bad Trip", in: Erections, Ejaculations, Exhibitions and General Tales of Ordinary Madness (1972); repr. Tales of Ordinary Madness (1983)
notes: Verified: Wikiquote lists it under Tales of Ordinary Madness and the Bukowski Forum pins it to the story "A Bad Trip".

quote: if you're going to try, go all the / way. / otherwise, don't even start. / if you're going to try, go all the / way. / this could mean losing girlfriends, / wives, relatives, jobs and / maybe your mind. / go all the way. / it could mean not eating for 3 or / 4 days. / it could mean freezing on a / park bench. / it could mean jail, / it could mean derision, / mockery, / isolation. / isolation is the gift, / all the others are a test of your / endurance, of / how much you really want to / do it. / and you'll do it / despite rejection and the worst odds / and it will be better than / anything else / you can imagine. / if you're going to try, / go all the way. / there is no other feeling like / that. / you will be alone with the gods / and the nights will flame with / fire. / do it, do it, do it. / do it. / all the way / all the way. / you will ride life straight to / perfect laughter, it's / the only good fight / there is.
author: Charles Bukowski
source_work: "roll the dice", in: What Matters Most Is How Well You Walk Through the Fire (1999), p. 408
notes: Wording as collected was: If you're going to try, go all the way. Otherwise, don't even start. This could mean losing girlfriends, wives, relatives and maybe even your mind. It could mean not eating for three or four days. It could mean freezing on a park bench. It could mean jail. It could mean derision. It could mean mockery - isolation. Isolation is the gift. All the others are a test of your endurance, of how much you really want to do it. And, you'll do it, despite rejection and the worst odds. And it will be better than anything else you can imagine. If you're going to try, go all the way. There is no other feeling like that. You will be alone with the gods, and the nights will flame with fire. You will ride life straight to perfect laughter. It's the only good fight there is. Wording corrected against the source: Genuine, but the bank drops "jobs" from the list of losses, drops the "do it, do it, do it" refrain and splits "derision, mockery, isolation" wrongly; text checked against the bukowski.net manuscript record and multiple concurring transcriptions.

quote: some people never go crazy, / what truly horrible lives / they must lead.
author: Charles Bukowski
source_work: "some people", in: Burning in Water, Drowning in Flame: Selected Poems 1955-1973 (1974)
notes: Wording as collected was: Some people never go crazy. What truly horrible lives they must live. Wording corrected against the source: The poem reads "lead", not "live"; verified in the book text, where the line also closes the poem rather than opening it.

quote: beware those who seek constant crowds for / they are nothing alone
author: Charles Bukowski
source_work: "The Genius of the Crowd" (1966), in: The Roominghouse Madrigals (1988), p. 31
notes: Wording as collected was: Beware of those who seek constant crowds; they are nothing alone. Wording corrected against the source: Genuine, but the poem has no "of" and runs on into the next line; checked against the poem text and the bukowskiforum.com works database.

quote: But your eyes - they're beautiful. They're wild, crazy, like some animal peering out of a forest on fire.
author: Charles Bukowski
notes: Verified: Verbatim in the novel, but it is spoken to Chinaski by a woman he has just met, not Bukowski describing someone else.

quote: And you invented me and I invented you and that's why we don't get along.
author: Charles Bukowski
source_work: "beds, toilets, you and me-", in: Love Is a Dog from Hell (1977), pp. 132-133
notes: Verified: Closing lines of the poem, verbatim in the book text.

quote: some people don't like him. some people don't like anybody who is famous and some people don't like anybody who isn't.
author: Charles Bukowski
notes: Wording as collected was: Some people don't like anybody who is famous. Some people don't like anybody who isn't. Wording corrected against the source: Genuine dialogue in the novel, but the two clauses are joined by "and" and follow "some people don't like him"; the bank turns one sentence into two.

quote: Can you remember who you were before the world told you who you should be?
author: Danielle LaPorte
source_work: Danielle LaPorte, The Fire Starter Sessions (2012)
notes: Previously attributed to Charles Bukowski. Reattributed: Not found anywhere in Bukowski; LaPorte's book is the documented source and libquotes/Goodreads attribute it to her.

quote: People with no morals often considered themselves more free, but mostly they lacked the ability to feel or to love.
author: Charles Bukowski
notes: Wording as collected was: People with no morals often considered themselves more free, but mostly they lacked the ability to feel or love. Wording corrected against the source: The novel reads "to feel or to love"; the bank drops the second "to" (Wikiquote's "feel hate or love" is also wrong against the book text).

quote: If somethings burns your soul with purpose and desire, it's your duty to be reduced to ashes by it. Any other form of existence will be yet another dull book in the library of life.
author: Andrea Balt
notes: Previously attributed to Charles Bukowski. Reattributed: Andrea Balt has publicly claimed this as her own writing; it appears in no Bukowski volume and is absent from his poetry and prose.

quote: I knew I was strong, and maybe like they said, Crazy. But I had this feeling inside of me that something real was there.
author: Charles Bukowski
notes: Verified: Verbatim in the novel; only difference is that the original has lower-case "crazy" in quotation marks.

quote: The crowd is the gathering place of the weakest, true creation is a solitary act.
author: Charles Bukowski
source_work: Interview reply, collected in: Sunlight Here I Am: Interviews and Encounters, 1963-1993 (2003)
notes: Verified: Genuine answer about poetry readings; the original uses a semicolon where the bank uses a comma.

quote: Some people like what you do, some people hate what you do, but most people simply don't give a damn.
author: Charles Bukowski
notes: Attribution unverified: Very widely circulated but no primary source in his books, letters or interviews could be located; it may well be a later aphorism pinned to his name.

quote: Goodness could be found sometimes in the middle of hell.
author: Charles Bukowski
notes: Wording as collected was: Goodness can be found. Sometimes in the middle of hell. Wording corrected against the source: The novel has one sentence in the past tense; the bank splits it in two and shifts to the present tense.

quote: Simplicity is always the secret, to a profound truth, to doing things, to writing, to painting. Life is profound in its simplicity.
author: Charles Bukowski
notes: Attribution unverified: Attributed to him all over quote sites but absent from the searchable corpus and from Wikiquote; no letter, poem or interview could be identified.

quote: Don't fight your demons. Your demons are here to teach you lessons. Sit down with your demons and have a drink and a chat and learn their names and talk about the birds on their fingers and scratches on their ankles. Some of them are very nice.
author: Charles Bukowski
notes: Attribution unverified: Absent from his books and interviews; the Bukowski Forum treats this "sit down with your demons" text as an internet invention in his voice.

quote: Understand me. I'm not like an ordinary world. I have my madness, I live in another dimension. And I have no time for things that have no soul.
author: Charles Bukowski
notes: Source spells 'Undestand'. Attribution unverified: No source in his work; this passage circulates only on quote sites and social media and reads as a translation-style pastiche. Also collected as: I have no time for things that have no soul. A fragment of a longer passage already held, from the same note and with the same unverified standing.

quote: Unless it comes out of your soul like a rocket, unless being still would drive you to madness or suicide or murder, don't do it. Unless the sun inside you is burning your gut, don't do it. When it is truly time, and if you have been chosen, it will do it by itself and it will keep on doing it until you die or it dies in you. There is no other way. And there never was.
author: Charles Bukowski
source_work: "so you want to be a writer?", in: Sifting Through the Madness for the Word, the Line, the Way: New Poems (2003), p. 3
notes: Verified: Every phrase matches the poem's text; the bank prints an elided excerpt of the closing sections.

quote: I am / a series of / small victories / and large defeats / and I am as / amazed / as any other / that / I have gotten / from there to / here
author: Charles Bukowski
source_work: "grip the dark", in: The People Look Like Flowers at Last: New Poems (2007), p. 49
notes: Wording as collected was: I am a series of small victories and large defeats and I am as amazed as any other that I have gotten from here to there. Wording corrected against the source: Genuine, but the poem reads "from there to here"; the bank reverses it, and the sentence continues "without committing murder".

quote: then something else in me said, no, save the tiniest / bit. / it needn't be much, just a spark. / a spark can set a whole forest on / fire. / just a spark. / save it.
author: Charles Bukowski
source_work: "spark", in: The Last Night of the Earth Poems (1992), pp. 158-159
notes: Wording as collected was: I was laying in bed one night and I thought: I'll just quit - to hell with it. And another little voice inside me said: Don't quit - save that tiny little ember of spark. And never give them that spark because as long as you have that spark, you can start the greatest fire again. Wording corrected against the source: The substance is genuinely his, from the poem "spark", but the prose version circulating online ("laying in bed one night", "start the greatest fire again") matches no located source. Wording as collected was: Save that tiny little ember of spark. And never give them that spark, because as long as you have that spark, you can start the greatest fire again. Wording corrected against the source: Same case: the sentiment and imagery are demonstrably his, but the "tiny little ember of spark" prose version has no locatable source. Also collected as: It needn't be much, just a spark. A spark can set a whole forest on fire. Just a spark. Save it. A prose flattening of the closing lines of the spark poem, already held in verse under the same citation.

quote: This is very important - To take leisure time. Pace is the essence. Without stopping entirely and doing nothing at all for great periods, you're gonna lose everything ... Just to do nothing at all.
author: Charles Bukowski
source_work: Interview by Sean Penn, "Tough Guys Write Poetry", Interview magazine (September 1987); collected in Sunlight Here I Am (2003)
notes: Verified: Matches the interview transcript exactly, including the elision the bank marks with an ellipsis.

quote: Invent yourself and then reinvent yourself.
author: Charles Bukowski
source_work: "no leaders, please"; verified in The Pleasures of the Damned: Poems 1951-1993 (2007)
notes: Verified: The poem opens "invent yourself and then reinvent yourself"; confirmed in the book text.

quote: Some lose all mind and become soul, insane. Some lose all soul and become mind, intellectual. Some lose both and become accepted.
author: Charles Bukowski
source_work: "lifedance", in: What Matters Most Is How Well You Walk Through the Fire (1999), p. 90
notes: Verified: Placement confirmed by the bukowskiforum.com works database; the bank substitutes commas for the original colons and omits the opening line about the brain and the soul.

quote: There may not be a hell, but those who judge may create one. I think people are over-taught. They are over-taught everything. You have to find out by what happens to you, how you will react. I'll have to use a strange term here ... "good." I don't know where it comes from, but I feel that there's an ultimate strain of goodness born in each of us. I don't believe in God, but I believe in this "goodness" like a tube running through our bodies. It can be nurtured. It's always magic, when on a freeway packed with traffic, a stranger makes room for you to change lanes ... it gives you hope.
author: Charles Bukowski
source_work: Interview by Sean Penn, "Tough Guys Write Poetry", Interview magazine (September 1987)
notes: Wording as collected was: There may not be a hell, but those who judge may create one. I think people are over-taught. They are over-taught everything. You have to find out by what happens to you, how you will react. I don't know where the term Good comes from, but I feel that there's an ultimate strain of Goodness born in each of us. I don't believe in god, but I believe in Goodness like a tube running through our bodies. It can be nurtured. It's always magic, when on a freeway packed with traffic, a stranger makes room for you to change lanes ... it gives you hope. Wording corrected against the source: Genuine, but the bank condenses his hesitation over the word "good" into "I don't know where the term Good comes from"; corrected against the interview transcript.

quote: You know the typical crowd, "Wow, it's Friday night, what are you going to do? Just sit there?" Well, yeah. Because there's nothing out there. It's stupidity. Stupid people mingling with stupid people. Let them stupidify themselves. I've never been bothered with the need to rush out into the night. I hid in bars, because I didn't want to hide in factories. That's all. Sorry for all the millions, but I've never been lonely. I like myself. I'm the best form of entertainment I have.
author: Charles Bukowski
source_work: Interview by Sean Penn, "Tough Guys Write Poetry", Interview magazine (September 1987)
notes: Wording as collected was: You know the typical crowd, wow, it's Friday night, what are you going to do? Just sit there? Well, yeah. Because there's nothing out there. It's stupidity. Stupid people mingling with stupid people. Let them stupidity themselves. I've never been bothered with the need to rush out into the night. That's all. Sorry for all the millions, but I've never been lonely. I like myself. I'm the best form of entertainment I have. Wording corrected against the source: Genuine, but the bank has "stupidity themselves" for his coinage "stupidify themselves" and drops the line about hiding in bars rather than factories.

quote: When you're a child you learn there are three dimensions: height, width and depth. Like a shoebox. Then later you hear there's a fourth dimension: time. Hmm. Then some say there can be five, six, seven... I knock off work, have a beer at the bar. I look down at the glass and feel glad.
author: Ron Padgett
source_work: Ron Padgett, 'Another One', one of four poems written for Jim Jarmusch's film Paterson (2016)
notes: Verified: poem 'Another One' written by Ron Padgett for Jim Jarmusch's film Paterson (2016). Verified: The poem is Padgett's own text that the film quotes, not a screenwriter's line, so the attribution stands. It is set as free verse: 'When you're a child / you learn / there are three dimensions: / height, width and depth. / Like a shoebox.' and so on. The bank runs it as prose, which is a formatting difference rather than a misquotation.

quote: But the first lesson reading teaches is how to be alone.
author: Jonathan Franzen
source_work: Jonathan Franzen, 'The Reader in Exile', The New Yorker, 6 March 1995; collected in How to Be Alone (Farrar, Straus and Giroux, 2002). It is the essay's last sentence
notes: Verified: Checked against the New Yorker text, where it closes the piece on Sven Birkerts and Nicholas Negroponte. The American Heritage Essential Student Thesaurus (2010) quotes it under 'lonely' with Franzen's name.

quote: Elective ignorance was a great survival skill, perhaps the greatest.
author: Jonathan Franzen
source_work: Jonathan Franzen, The Corrections (Farrar, Straus and Giroux, 2001), in the passage on everything one refuses 'to relish or discover'
notes: Verified: Five Internet Archive printings of the novel give the sentence verbatim, preceded by 'he just might die of boredom'. Richard Cox's The God Particle (2005) quotes it as a line from a recent American novel.

quote: Fiction is a solution, the best solution, to the problem of existential solitude.
author: Jonathan Franzen
source_work: Jonathan Franzen, 'Farther Away', The New Yorker, 18 April 2011; collected in Farther Away: Essays (Farrar, Straus and Giroux, 2012) and in The Best American Essays 2012
notes: Verified: The essay on David Foster Wallace and Robinson Crusoe; the book text reads 'fiction is a solution, the best solution, to the problem of existential solitude. Fiction was his way off the island', so the bank has the clause exactly.

quote: How wrong to have been so negative, how wrong to have been so gloomy, how wrong to have run away from life, how wrong to have said no, again and again, instead of yes.
author: Jonathan Franzen
source_work: Jonathan Franzen, The Corrections (Farrar, Straus and Giroux, 2001), the regret passage running 'so much time at work and so little with the children'
notes: Verified: Six Internet Archive printings carry the sentence word for word as the bank has it, and Judith Viorst quotes the passage in Grown-Up Marriage (2003).

quote: All those moments will be lost in time, like tears in rain.
author: Roy Batty
source_work: Blade Runner (1982), directed by Ridley Scott, the replicant Roy Batty's dying speech on the rooftop; screenplay by Hampton Fancher and David Peoples
notes: Spoken by the character Roy Batty; line partly improvised by Rutger Hauer. Reattributed: The words belong to the character, not to the actor speaking in his own voice. Rutger Hauer played Batty and cut the speech down himself on the night, which he describes in his memoir All Those Moments (2007); the film's wording matches the bank's exactly.

quote: No sympathy for the devil; keep that in mind. Buy the ticket, take the ride... and if it occasionally gets a little heavier than what you had in mind, well... maybe chalk it up to forced consciousness expansion: Tune in, freak out, get beaten.
author: Hunter S. Thompson
source_work: Hunter S. Thompson, Fear and Loathing in Las Vegas (Random House, 1971), in the passage beginning 'The possibility of physical and mental collapse is now very real'
notes: Verified: The 1971 and 1982 printings both carry the passage verbatim, ellipsis and all, down to the closing 'Tune in, freak out, get beaten'.

quote: We are what we pretend to be, so we must be careful about what we pretend to be.
author: Kurt Vonnegut
source_work: Kurt Vonnegut, Mother Night, the author's Introduction added to the 1966 edition
notes: Verified: Vonnegut offers it there as the moral of the book. The critical literature (The Critical Response to Kurt Vonnegut, 1994; New Critical Essays on Kurt Vonnegut, 2009) quotes it in exactly this form, occasionally without 'about'.

quote: I hope to stay light on my feet, to work in many modes, to seek inspiration always, and avoid the fatal. But, as we all know, it is the price of life to burn out, both metaphorically and literally.
author: T.C. Boyle
source_work: T. C. Boyle, interview with The Talks (the-talks.com), answering the question 'Do you think you'll ever burn out?'
notes: Verified: The published answer runs 'Burn out? A terrifying term to a committed artist. I hope to stay light on my feet, to work in many modes, to seek inspiration always, and avoid the fatal. But, as we all know, it is the price of life to burn out, both metaphorically and literally.' The bank has the last two sentences word for word.

quote: What is your identity, and how do you know who you are if you don't have language?
author: T.C. Boyle
notes: Attribution unverified: No printed occurrence in the Internet Archive corpus, and on the web the sentence appears only on quote-scraping sites. Boyle makes the same point in his own words about Talk Talk - 'probing the question of what our identity is and how we know ourselves through language' in the readers' guide on tcboyle.com, and 'the question of identity and the language by which we define ourselves' in his 2006 Web del Sol interview - but this exact sentence could not be located in any interview or book.

quote: The only obsession everyone wants: love. People think that in falling in love they make themselves whole? The Platonic union of souls? I think otherwise. I think you're whole before you begin. And the love fractures you. You're whole, and then you're cracked open.
author: Philip Roth
source_work: Philip Roth, The Dying Animal (Houghton Mifflin, 2001), George O'Hearn's tirade against falling in love, addressed to David Kepesh
notes: Verified: The novel reads 'you're whole before you begin. And the love fractures you. You're whole, and then you're cracked open'. Mark Shechner's Up Society's Ass, Copper (2003) quotes the same passage and names George O'Hearn as the speaker.

quote: There's no remaking reality... Just take it as it comes. Hold your ground and take it as it comes. There's no other way.
author: Philip Roth
source_work: Philip Roth, Everyman (Houghton Mifflin, 2006), the protagonist saying it back to his daughter Nancy
notes: Verified: The text reads 'But there's no remaking reality,' he said softly, rubbing her back, followed by 'Just take it as it comes. Hold your ground and take it as it comes. There's no other way.' The bank's ellipsis stitches together the two halves of one speech, and the words are exact. The maxim first appears in the book in Nancy's mouth at the graveside.

quote: You be greater than your feelings. I don't demand this of you - life does. Otherwise you'll be washed away by feelings. You'll be washed out to sea and never seen again.
author: Philip Roth
source_work: Philip Roth, Indignation (Houghton Mifflin, 2008), Marcus Messner's mother, in the speech beginning 'your father is as bad as the rest of them'
notes: Verified: Three Internet Archive printings carry the passage verbatim: 'Don't you be. You be greater than your feelings. I don't demand this of you - life does. Otherwise you'll be washed away by feelings. You'll be washed out to sea and never seen again.'

quote: The danger with hatred is, once you start in on it, you get a hundred times more than you bargained for. Once you start, you can't stop.
author: Philip Roth
source_work: Philip Roth, The Human Stain (Houghton Mifflin, 2000)
notes: Verified: Four Internet Archive copies, including the 2011 American Trilogy omnibus, read 'He goes out of his way to make it easy for you. But the danger with hatred is, once you start in on it, you get a hundred times more than you bargained for. Once you start, you can't stop.' The bank has the two sentences exactly.

quote: Pain is like a baby crying. What it wants it can't name.
author: Philip Roth
source_work: Philip Roth, The Anatomy Lesson (Farrar, Straus and Giroux, 1983), the passage on dolorologists
notes: Verified: The 1983 and 1984 printings both read 'clinical intuition. Pain is like a baby crying. What it wants it can't name. The dolorologist unearths what that...', so the bank has the sentences verbatim.

quote: There is truth and then again there is truth. For all that the world is full of people who go around believing they've got you or your neighbour figured out, there really is no bottom to what is not known. The truth about us is endless. As are the lies.
author: Philip Roth
source_work: Philip Roth, The Human Stain (Houghton Mifflin, 2000), Nathan Zuckerman's narration
notes: Verified: Quoted verbatim and credited to The Human Stain in Jewish Choices, Jewish Voices (2009); Christopher Peterson's Bestial Traces (2013) identifies the voice as Nathan's. The bank's text, ending 'The truth about us is endless. As are the lies,' matches.

quote: You have a conscience, and a conscience is a valuable attribute, but not if it begins to make you think you were to blame for what is far beyond the scope of your responsibility.
author: Philip Roth
source_work: Philip Roth, Nemesis (Houghton Mifflin, 2010), Dr Steinberg to Bucky Cantor
notes: Verified: The Chambers Dictionary of Great Quotations carries the sentence in exactly the bank's wording, 'to make you think you were to blame for what is far beyond the scope of your responsibility', which the novel's text confirms; Bucky's unspoken reply, 'Doesn't God have a conscience?', follows.

quote: You tasted it. Isn't that enough? Of what do you ever get more than a taste? That's all we're given in life, that's all we're given of life. A taste. There is no more.
author: Philip Roth
source_work: Philip Roth, The Dying Animal (Houghton Mifflin, 2001), George O'Hearn on his deathbed
notes: Verified: The novel reads 'A taste. There is no more,' with the narrator adding 'George was right, of course' afterwards. The bank's four sentences are verbatim.

quote: How easy life is when it's easy, and how hard when it's hard.
author: Philip Roth
source_work: Philip Roth, The Professor of Desire (Farrar, Straus and Giroux, 1977), David Kepesh's narration, just before Claire is introduced
notes: Verified: Three Internet Archive printings read 'My, how easy life is when it's easy, and how hard when it's hard!' The bank drops the opening interjection and the exclamation mark; the sentence itself is word for word.

quote: Actually we did not have the feelings we said we had until we spoke them - at least I didn't; to phrase them was to invent them and own them.
author: Philip Roth
notes: Verified: Confirmed verbatim in the full text of Goodbye, Columbus.

quote: Life should not be a journey to the grave with the intention of arriving safely in a pretty and well preserved body, but rather to skid in broadside in a cloud of smoke, thoroughly used up, totally worn out, and loudly proclaiming Wow! What a Ride!
author: Hunter S. Thompson
notes: Attribution unverified: Quote Investigator finds this is NOT Thompson's: it is anonymous, first appearing on Usenet in October 1998, and is absent from The Proud Highway and Gonzo (the very books it is credited to). Sometimes credited to motorcycle racer Bill McKenna (Cycle, 1982) but uncertain.

quote: We are all alone, born alone, die alone, and - in spite of true romance magazines - we shall all someday look back on our lives and see that, in spite of our company, we were alone the whole way. I do not say lonely - at least, not all the time - but essentially, and finally, alone. This is what makes your self-respect so important, and I don't see how you can respect yourself if you must look in the hearts and minds of others for your happiness.
author: Hunter S. Thompson
source_work: Hunter S. Thompson, The Proud Highway (letter to Hume Logan, 22 April 1958)
notes: Verified: Genuinely from Thompson's celebrated 1958 letter of advice to Hume Logan, collected in The Proud Highway (original reads 'True Romance magazines', a magazine title).

quote: A man who procrastinates in his choosing, will inevitably have his choice made for him by circumstance.
author: Hunter S. Thompson
source_work: Hunter S. Thompson, The Proud Highway (letter to Hume Logan, 22 April 1958)
notes: Verified: From the same 1958 Hume Logan letter in The Proud Highway.

quote: Life has improved immeasurably since I have been forced to stop taking it seriously.
author: Hunter S. Thompson
source_work: The Proud Highway: Saga of a Desperate Southern Gentleman 1955-1967 (1997), letter to Eleanor McGarr, 28 August 1962
notes: Wording as collected was: Life has become immeasurably better since I have been forced to stop taking it seriously. Wording corrected against the source: Internet Archive full-text search finds the bank's wording only in later quote books; Thompson's own letter, printed in The Proud Highway and in The Fear and Loathing Letters vol. 1 (both 1997, p. 726 of the scan), reads 'Life has improved immeasurably', not 'Life has become immeasurably better'.

quote: Let us toast to animal pleasures, to escapism, to rain on the roof and instant coffee, to unemployment insurance and library cards, to absinthe and good-hearted landlords, to music and warm bodies and contraceptives... and to the good life, whatever it is and wherever it happens to be.
author: Hunter S. Thompson
source_work: Hunter S. Thompson, The Proud Highway (1997), p. 101
notes: Verified: From one of Thompson's letters in The Proud Highway; located at p. 101.

quote: If you're going to be crazy, you have to get paid for it or else you're going to be locked up.
author: Hunter S. Thompson
source_work: Interview collected in Ancient Gonzo Wisdom: Interviews with Hunter S. Thompson, ed. Anita Thompson (2009), p. 438
notes: Verified: Found verbatim in Thompson's own collected interviews via Internet Archive full-text search; the page carries a 'Playboy, May 2005' source line. Wording matches the bank exactly.

quote: Some may never live, but the crazy never die.
author: Hunter S. Thompson
notes: Attribution unverified: Attributed to Thompson only on quote aggregators, with no primary source located; it may derive from the 1980 film Where the Buffalo Roam rather than Thompson's writing.

quote: All my life, my heart has sought a thing I cannot name.
author: Hunter S. Thompson
source_work: Hunter S. Thompson, Hell's Angels (1966) - epigraph
notes: Source notes 'Remembered line from a long-forgotten poem'. Verified: The line does appear in Hell's Angels as Thompson used it, but he labelled it 'Remembered line from a long-forgotten...' source, so the words may not be original to him.

quote: Freedom is something that dies unless it's used.
author: Hunter S. Thompson
source_work: Hunter S. Thompson (interview, collected in Ancient Gonzo Wisdom)
notes: Verified: A documented Thompson remark from his interviews (Ancient Gonzo Wisdom: Interviews with Hunter S. Thompson).

quote: The really important kind of freedom involves attention, and awareness, and discipline, and effort, and being able truly to care about other people and to sacrifice for them, over and over, in myriad petty little unsexy ways, every day.
author: David Foster Wallace
source_work: David Foster Wallace, This Is Water (2005 Kenyon address; pub. 2009)
notes: From David Foster Wallace's 'This Is Water' (2005 Kenyon commencement); the source file misattributed it to Jonathan Franzen. Wording as collected was: The really important kind of freedom involves attention and awareness and discipline, and being able truly to care about other people and to sacrifice for them, over and over, in myriad petty little unsexy ways, every day. Wording corrected against the source: Genuine DFW, but the bank drops 'and effort' from the list ('attention, and awareness, and discipline, and effort'). Restored against the text of This Is Water.

quote: The love that anyone can have for you is always conditional.
author: Jonathan Franzen
notes: Attribution unverified: Attributed to Jonathan Franzen only on quote aggregators (Bookey, Goodreads) with no source citation; not located in the book corpus. Plausibly his but unconfirmed.

quote: Ultimately, the only way to be happy is to care deeply about the things that should be cared about and not caring, not at all, about the things that shouldn't be cared about.
author: Jonathan Franzen
notes: Attribution unverified: Attributed to Franzen only on aggregators, with no primary source and no match in the book corpus.

quote: Sometimes loving someone means letting them be free to be the villains they are trying to become.
author: Jonathan Franzen
notes: Attribution unverified: Attributed to Franzen only on aggregators (Bookey), with no identifiable source work; not found in the book corpus.

quote: The feeling of being hurried is not usually the result of living a life that is full and important; it is, on the contrary, born of a vague and oppressive sense of resentment that something vital is missing.
author: Eric Hoffer
source_work: Eric Hoffer, Reflections on the Human Condition (1973), p. 124
notes: Previously attributed to Jonathan Franzen. Reattributed: Not Franzen: this is Eric Hoffer's aphorism. Hoffer's wording ends 'it is, on the contrary, born of a vague fear that we are wasting our life'; the bank's ending ('...resentment that something vital is missing') is a loose paraphrase. Author corrected to Hoffer.

quote: There is, after all, a kind of happiness in unhappiness, if it's the right unhappiness.
author: Jonathan Franzen
notes: Verified: Confirmed verbatim in the full text of Franzen's novel Freedom.

quote: Go for broke. Always try and do too much. Dispense with safety nets. Take a deep breath before you begin talking. Aim for the stars. Keep grinning. Be bloody-minded. Argue with the world. And never forget that writing is as close as we get to keeping a hold on the thousand and one things - childhood, certainties, cities, doubts, dreams, instants, phrases, parents, loves - that go on slipping, like sand, through our fingers.
author: Salman Rushdie
source_work: Salman Rushdie, 'Imaginary Homelands' (1982), in Imaginary Homelands (1991)
notes: Verified: Confirmed as Rushdie's from the title essay of Imaginary Homelands; quoted verbatim in writing guides.

quote: What's real and what's true aren't necessarily the same.
author: Salman Rushdie
notes: Verified: Confirmed as a line from Midnight's Children (Rushdie 1981), cited verbatim in scholarly studies of the novel.

quote: Your task is not to seek for love, but merely to seek and find all the barriers within yourself that you have built against it.
author: Helen Schucman
source_work: A Course in Miracles (1976), Text ch. 16.IV.6
notes: Previously attributed to Rumi. Reattributed: The line is verbatim from A Course in Miracles and has no counterpart in Rumi's Persian, as Quote Investigator has documented.

quote: Stop acting so small. You are the universe in ecstatic motion.
author: Rumi
notes: Attribution unverified: Universally credited to The Essential Rumi but absent from the full text of that book, and no Persian counterpart could be found.

quote: Yesterday I was clever, so I wanted to change the world. Today I am wise, so I am changing myself.
author: Rumi
notes: Attribution unverified: A modern self-help antithesis with no counterpart in the Masnavi, Divan or quatrains; not present in Barks either.

quote: Don't grieve. Anything you lose comes round in another form.
author: Rumi
notes: Renders the source loosely: Coleman Barks' version "Unmarked Boxes" in The Essential Rumi, whose own reference list gives ghazal 1937; Persian wording not confirmed so left blank.

quote: The minute I heard my first love story, I started looking for you, not knowing how blind that was. Lovers don't finally meet somewhere. They're in each other all along.
author: Rumi
notes: Renders the source loosely: Barks' version in The Essential Rumi ch. 8, sourced in his own reference list to quatrain 1246; Persian wording not confirmed so left blank.

quote: Don't be satisfied with stories, how things have gone with others. Unfold your own myth.
author: Rumi
notes: Renders the source loosely: Barks' version "Unfold Your Own Myth" in The Essential Rumi ch. 4, sourced in his reference list to ghazal 598; Persian wording not confirmed.

quote: Dance, when you're broken open. Dance, if you've torn the bandage off. Dance in the middle of the fighting. Dance in your blood. Dance when you're perfectly free.
author: Rumi
notes: Renders the source loosely: Barks' quatrain-section version in The Essential Rumi p. 281, which his own notes cite to Masnavi III 95-97; I could not confirm the Persian wording.

quote: If you are irritated by every rub, how will your mirror be polished?
author: Rumi
notes: Verified: Wikiquote sources this to Masnavi I 2980 (tr. Helminski, Daylight, 1990), and Nicholson renders the same verse almost identically; Persian not obtained.

quote: You were born with wings, why prefer to crawl through life?
author: Rumi
notes: Attribution unverified: Wikiquote can trace it no further than Larry Chang's 2006 anthology, and no Persian counterpart could be located.

quote: Forget safety. Live where you fear to live. Destroy your reputation. Be notorious.
author: Rumi
notes: Renders the source loosely: Barks' version "Feeling the Shoulder of the Lion", reproduced with this Masnavi citation in multiple independent sources; Persian wording not confirmed.

quote: Everything in the universe is within you. Ask all from yourself.
author: Majd al-Din Baghdadi
source_work: Quatrain printed as Rumi Rubaiyat no. 1759; ascribed to Majd al-Din Baghdadi in Nuzhat al-Majalis
notes: Previously attributed to Rumi. Reattributed: Ganjoor flags this quatrain as attributed to several poets, the earliest anthology naming Majd al-Din Baghdadi, with Baba Afzal Kashani also proposed.

quote: Set your life on fire. Seek those who fan your flames.
author: Rumi
notes: Attribution unverified: Modern motivational English with no counterpart in the Masnavi, Divan or quatrains and no presence in Barks' published versions.

quote: A thousand half-loves must be forsaken to take one whole heart home.
author: Rumi
notes: Attribution unverified: Quote aggregators cite only Raficq Abdulla's loose interpretations in Words of Paradise with no poem or page, and no Persian counterpart was found.

quote: You have to keep breaking your heart until it opens.
author: Rumi
notes: Attribution unverified: Circulates as a Barks line but is absent from the full text of The Essential Rumi, and no Persian counterpart could be located.

quote: I was fighting a small fight of my own which wasn't leading anywhere - but like a man with a bent spoon trying to dig through a cement wall I knew that a small fight was better than quitting. It kept the heart alive.
author: Charles Bukowski
notes: Verified: Verbatim in the book text; the original has a colon before "it kept the heart alive".

quote: Nobody can save you but yourself and you're worth saving. It's a war not easily won but if anything is worth winning then this is it.
author: Charles Bukowski
source_work: "nobody but you", in: Sifting Through the Madness for the Word, the Line, the Way: New Poems (2003), p. 393
notes: Verified: Both sentences appear verbatim in the poem's closing movement.

quote: My dear, find what you love and let it kill you. Let it drain you of your all. Let it cling onto your back and weigh you down into eventual nothingness. Let it kill you and let it devour your remains. For all things will kill you, both slowly and fastly, but it's much better to be killed by a lover.
notes: Popularly misattributed to Bukowski (no verified source); the core line 'find what you love and let it kill you' is credited to Kinky Friedman (1986). This extended version is apocryphal. Attribution unverified: Widely misattributed to Charles Bukowski, but Quote Investigator finds no such poem or story; a 'find what you LIKE' variant belongs to Kinky Friedman. The longer 'My dear...' passage is of unknown origin. The bank's 'Unknown' is correct.

quote: And when love came to us twice and lied to us twice we decided to never love again, that was fair; fair to us and fair to love itself. We ask for no mercy or no miracles; we are strong enough to live and to die and to kill flies, attend the boxing matches, go to the racetrack, live on luck and skill, get alone, get alone often, and if you can't sleep alone be careful of the words you speak in your sleep; and ask for no mercy no miracles; and don't forget: time is meant to be wasted, love fails and death is useless.
author: Charles Bukowski
source_work: "time is made to be wasted" (c. 1978), in: Dangling in the Tournefortia (1981), p. 89
notes: Verified: Poem identified via the bukowski.net poem database; the bank prints the verse flattened into prose but the wording is accurate.

quote: Art takes discipline. Any asshole can chase a skirt.
author: Charles Bukowski
notes: Wording as collected was: Any asshole can chase a skirt, art takes discipline. Wording corrected against the source: Genuine, but the novel puts the two sentences the other way round, as two full sentences rather than a comma splice.

quote: To create art means to be crazy alone forever.
author: Charles Bukowski
notes: Attribution unverified: Circulates only on quote sites; not present in the searchable corpus of his poetry and prose and not in Wikiquote, but I could not identify another author either.

quote: Style is the answer to everything. A fresh way to approach a dull or dangerous thing. To do a dull thing with style is preferable to doing a dangerous thing without it. To do a dangerous thing with style is what I call art.
author: Charles Bukowski
source_work: "style", in: Mockingbird Wish Me Luck (1972), p. 155
notes: Verified: Confirmed in the book, though the printed 1972 text stops at "without it"; the fourth sentence belongs to the longer version Bukowski recited, familiar from Tales of Ordinary Madness (1981).

quote: And don't forget: time is meant to be wasted, love fails and death is useless.
author: Charles Bukowski
source_work: "time is made to be wasted" (c. 1978), in: Dangling in the Tournefortia (1981), p. 89
notes: Verified: The closing line of the same poem, quoted accurately.

quote: I am not a snob; it is simply that I am not interested with what most people have to say, or what they want to do - mostly with my time.
author: Charles Bukowski
source_work: Notes of a Dirty Old Man (1969)
notes: Verified: Found verbatim in the book, including the unidiomatic "not interested with what most people have to say"; the bank's wording is his, not an error.

quote: Those faces you see every day on the streets were not created entirely without hope: be kind to them: like you they have not escaped.
author: Charles Bukowski
source_work: "a plausible finish", in: The People Look Like Flowers at Last: New Poems (2007), p. 201
notes: Verified: Closing lines of the poem, verbatim; the bank prints the verse as prose.

quote: Love is kind of like when you see a fog in the morning, when you wake up before the sun comes out. It's just a little while, and then it burns away... Love is a fog that burns with the first daylight of reality.
author: Charles Bukowski
source_work: Filmed interview reply to the question "What is your definition of love?"
notes: Verified: The spoken answer ends "Love is a fog that burns with the first daylight of reality"; the bank matches the standard transcription, though the original said "it's just there a little while".

quote: Are you becoming what you've always hated?
author: Charles Bukowski
notes: Attribution unverified: Common on quote images but I found no poem, story, letter or interview containing it, and no alternative author.

quote: We are here to laugh at the odds and live our lives so well that death will tremble to take us.
author: Charles Bukowski
source_work: "The Meaning of Life: The Big Picture", Life magazine (December 1988)
notes: Verified: This closing sentence is quoted with its source on Wikiquote and matches the bank exactly.

quote: drink from the well / of your self / and begin / again.
author: Charles Bukowski
source_work: "mind and heart"; verified in The Pleasures of the Damned: Poems 1951-1993 (2007)
notes: Wording as collected was: Drink from the well of yourself and begin again. Wording corrected against the source: Genuine closing lines, but the poem writes "your self" as two words, echoing "the well of my self" earlier in the same poem.

quote: If you're going to try, go all the way. There is no other feeling like that. You will be alone with the gods, and the nights will flame with fire. You will ride life straight to perfect laughter. It's the only good fight there is.
author: Charles Bukowski
source_work: "roll the dice", in: What Matters Most Is How Well You Walk Through the Fire (1999), p. 408
notes: Excerpt of the longer 'go all the way' passage. Verified: An accurate elided excerpt of the poem's final movement; every word matches.

quote: Love is a form of prejudice. You love what you need, you love what makes you feel good, you love what is convenient. How can you say you love one person when there are ten thousand people in the world that you would love more if you ever met them? But you'll never meet them.
author: Charles Bukowski
notes: Attribution unverified: Only "Love is a form of prejudice. I have too many other prejudices." is confirmed, in Women (1978) ch. 80; the long expansion about ten thousand people appears in no text I could search and is variously credited to Women and Hot Water Music.

quote: We waited and waited. All of us. Didn't the shrink know that waiting was one of the things that drove people crazy? People waited all their lives. They waited to live, they waited to die. They waited in line to buy toilet paper. They waited in line for money. And if they didn't have any money they waited in longer lines. You waited to go to sleep and then you waited to awaken. You waited to get married and you waited to get divorced. You waited for it to rain, you waited for it to stop. You waited to eat and then you waited to eat again. You waited in a shrink's office with a bunch of psychos and you wondered if you were one.
author: Charles Bukowski
notes: Wording as collected was: Are people crazy? People waited all their lives. They waited to live, they waited to die. They waited in line to buy toilet paper. They waited in line for money. And if they didn't have any money they waited in longer lines. You waited to go to sleep and then you waited to awaken. You waited to get married and you waited to get divorced. You waited for it to rain, you waited for it to stop. You waited to eat and then you waited to eat again. You waited in a shrink's office with a bunch of psychos and you wondered if you were one. Wording corrected against the source: Genuine, from the psychiatrist's waiting room in Pulp, but the bank replaces the real opening with an invented question, "Are people crazy?".

quote: For those who believe in God, most of the big questions are answered. But for those of us who can't readily accept the God formula, the big answers don't remain stone-written. We adjust to new conditions and discoveries. We are pliable. Love need not be a command nor faith a dictum. I am my own god. We are here to unlearn the teachings of the church, state, and our educational system. We are here to drink beer. We are here to kill war. We are here to laugh at the odds and live our lives so well that death will tremble to take us.
author: Charles Bukowski
source_work: "The Meaning of Life: The Big Picture", Life magazine (December 1988)
notes: Verified: Source and wording confirmed on Wikiquote; the only divergences are "nor faith a dictum" for "or faith a dictum" and the hyphen in "stone-written", too slight to call a rewording.

quote: Success is getting what you want. Happiness is wanting what you get.
author: Dale Carnegie
notes: Attribution unverified: Consistently attributed to Dale Carnegie but with no primary source in his works; a floating aphorism found only on quote sites.

quote: Without deviation from the norm, progress is not possible.
author: Frank Zappa
source_work: The Real Frank Zappa Book (1989), ch. 8 'All About Music'
notes: Verified: Zappa quotes himself there: 'One of the things I have said before in interviews is: "Without deviation (from the norm), 'progress' is not possible."' Confirmed in the Internet Archive full text of the book; the remark goes back to his interview in Roelof Kiers's VPRO documentary, broadcast 11 February 1971.

quote: The universe consists of 5% protons, 5% neutrons, 5% electrons and 85% morons.
author: Frank Zappa
notes: Attribution unverified: A joke-format line attributed to Frank Zappa with no source in any of his writings or interviews; appears nowhere in the book corpus and reads as an internet-era fabrication.

quote: The shoe that fits one person pinches another; there is no recipe for living that suits all cases.
author: Carl Jung
source_work: Ziele der Psychotherapie (1931), in: Seelenprobleme der Gegenwart; engl. CW 16 § 81
notes: Verified: Located verbatim in CW 16 § 81 in the Baynes-Dell wording (the later CW revision reads no universal recipe for living), but the German sentence could not be checked against a primary text, so it is left blank.

quote: Es kann keinen Flug geben ohne vorangegangene Träume vom Fliegen.
author: Stanisław Lem
notes: Attribution unverified: Credited to Lem in German collections and used as the motto of a Lem biography, but neither a passage in his work nor a Polish original can be traced.

quote: There can be no flight without preceding dreams of flying.
author: Stanisław Lem
notes: English translation of the Polish/German original. The text this renders does not exist in the language it was written in, so the same finding applies here.

quote: Never apologize for showing feeling. When you do so, you apologize for truth.
author: Benjamin Disraeli
source_work: Contarini Fleming: A Psychological Romance (1832), Part I, ch. 13
notes: Renders the source loosely: Checked the 1832 first edition and the 1850 Works of D'Israeli the Younger on the Internet Archive: 'Never apologize for showing feeling, my friend. Remember that when you do so, you apologize for truth.' The bank's line is that sentence with the address and 'Remember that' dropped; nothing is misstated.

quote: It all depends on how we look at things, and not how they are in themselves.
author: Carl Jung
source_work: Ziele der Psychotherapie (1931), in: Seelenprobleme der Gegenwart; engl. CW 16 § 96
notes: Verified: Located verbatim in CW 16 § 96 of the full text of The Practice of Psychotherapy, but of the German only the following sentence Kleinstes mit Sinn ist immer lebenswerter als Größtes ohne Sinn is attested, so the original is left blank.

quote: One fails forward toward success.
author: Charles Kettering
source_work: Prophet of Progress: Selections from the Speeches of Charles F. Kettering, ed. T. A. Boyd (1961), p. 237; also p. 268, 'In research, one fails forward toward success'
notes: Verified: Found in the collected selections from Kettering's own speeches on the Internet Archive, where the sentence stands verbatim after 'Failures, repeated failures, are finger posts on the road to achievement.' Quote books frequently reassign the line to C. S. Lewis.

quote: In seed time learn, in harvest teach, in winter enjoy.
author: William Blake
source_work: William Blake, 'Proverbs of Hell', The Marriage of Heaven and Hell (c.1790)
notes: Verified: Confirmed verbatim as one of Blake's Proverbs of Hell.

quote: You are what you do, not what you say you do.
author: Carl Jung
notes: Attribution unverified: Not present in the searchable full text of Jung's Collected Works and circulated only by quote aggregators such as Goodreads, always without a source.

quote: Shoot for the moon. Even if you miss, you'll land among the stars.
author: Les Brown
notes: Verified: Per Quote Investigator, this exact 'shoot for the moon' wording is credited to Les Brown (by 2000, and in The Dictionary of Modern Proverbs); the underlying celestial-aim adage is older (W. Clement Stone, Norman Vincent Peale, P.T. Barnum).

quote: You can stand tall without standing on someone. You can be a victor without having victims.
author: Harriet Woods
notes: Attribution unverified: The earliest traceable appearance is Carolyn Warner, The Last Word: A Treasury of Women's Quotes (1992), p. 147, which cites no source; Wikiquote's sourced entry goes no further than that book. Internet Archive full-text search returns 38 printings, every one a gift book or quote anthology from 1994 on. Also circulates misattributed to Harriet Beecher Stowe.

quote: To be wronged is nothing unless you continue to remember it.
author: Confucius
notes: Attribution unverified: No such saying in the Analects or the other classics; it appears only in modern English quotation books, as Wikiquote's Confucius misattributed section notes.

quote: When in doubt, tell the truth.
author: Mark Twain
source_work: Mark Twain, Following the Equator (1897), Pudd'nhead Wilson's New Calendar
notes: Verified: A genuine Twain maxim from Following the Equator, confirmed in The Wit & Wisdom of Mark Twain.

quote: Mögest du immer Rückenwind haben und stets Sonnenschein im Gesicht. Und mögen die Schicksalsstürme dich hinauftragen, auf dass du mit den Sternen tanzt.
author: Traditional Irish Blessing
notes: German version of the Irish blessing. Attribution unverified: The traditional Irish blessing runs "May the road rise up to meet you ..."; the line about dancing with the stars is a modern anonymous addition with no transmitted source.

quote: May the wind always be at your back and the sun upon your face and may the wings of destiny carry you aloft to dance with the stars.
author: Traditional Irish Blessing
notes: The text this renders does not exist in the language it was written in, so the same finding applies here.
